entities.name: Lothair I
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lothair I (c. 795 – 855), the eldest son of Emperor Louis the Pious, emerged as a pivotal figure in the 9th-century Carolingian Empire, whose reign as co-Emperor (817–840), Emperor (840–855), King of Italy (818–855), and King of Middle Francia (843–855) fundamentally reshaped the political landscape of Western Europe. His tumultuous career, marked by persistent fratricidal conflicts with his brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald, directly led to the fracturing of the vast Carolingian realm established by his grandfather Charlemagne, laying the groundwork for the future kingdoms of France and Germany. He embodied the complex challenges of imperial succession and the struggle to maintain a unified Christian empire in the face of burgeoning regional identities and powerful aristocratic factions.

Lothair’s political trajectory was largely defined by the "Ordinatio Imperii" of 817, which designated him as the primary heir and co-emperor, granting his younger brothers subordinate kingdoms. However, the subsequent birth of Charles the Bald and Louis the Pious’s attempts to revise the succession sparked decades of civil war. A key event was the Battle of Fontenoy in 841, where Lothair's forces were decisively defeated by the combined armies of Louis and Charles, significantly weakening his imperial authority. This defeat culminated in the pivotal Treaty of Verdun in 843, which formally partitioned the Carolingian Empire into three distinct kingdoms: West Francia for Charles the Bald, East Francia for Louis the German, and Middle Francia (a long, narrow strip from the North Sea to Italy, including the imperial capitals of Aachen and Rome) for Lothair. His imperial title, though still held, lost much of its universal authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lothair I's relentless struggle for imperial supremacy directly led to the Treaty of Verdun in 843, which irrevocably partitioned the Carolingian Empire into three distinct kingdoms, foundational to the modern states of France, Germany, and Italy. His reign marks the definitive end of a unified Frankish empire and the beginning of a new geopolitical order in Western Europe.
